title: Forgiveness, Mercy, and the Harvest
summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls the tax collector Matthew, and eats with tax collectors and sinners, defending himself with the words of Hosea. He answers a question about fasting, raises a synagogue leader's daughter, heals a woman who touches his cloak, gives sight to two blind men, and frees a mute man. Moved by the crowds, he tells his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest.
story: This chapter completes the cycle of ten miracles that Matthew began in chapter 8, and it raises the stakes. Jesus now claims authority not only over disease and storm but over sin itself, which his critics recognize as a claim that belongs to God. Opposition appears for the first time in earnest: scribes think he blasphemes, Pharisees object to his table companions, and at the end they explain his power as the work of the prince of demons. At the same time the circle of followers widens to include a despised tax collector. The closing scene, with Jesus' compassion for crowds like sheep without a shepherd, leads straight into chapter 10, where he sends out the twelve.
historical:
Capernaum, Jesus' own town (verse 1), stood near the border between the territory of Herod Antipas and that of his brother Philip, and near a road that carried trade around the lake. That setting explains Matthew's tax booth. Under Antipas, tolls and customs on goods were collected by local men who bought or held the right to collect and made their living from what they took in above the required amount. Such collectors were widely regarded as dishonest and as collaborators with the ruling powers, and Jewish sources group them with sinners and robbers. Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 call the man Levi, while this Gospel calls him Matthew and lists him among the twelve in 10:3 as Matthew the tax collector. Most interpreters take Levi and Matthew as two names for the same man.

The Pharisees were a lay movement within Judaism devoted to careful keeping of the law of Moses, including the purity rules that governed meals, and they had wide respect among ordinary people. The scribes were experts in the law who taught and interpreted it; many were Pharisees. John the Baptist's disciples, who were still active while their teacher was in prison, practiced regular fasting, as did the Pharisees, who according to Luke 18:12 fasted twice a week.
cultural:
Sharing a meal in the ancient world meant accepting the people at the table, and for Pharisees careful about purity it mattered greatly who one ate with. Jesus' dinner with tax collectors and sinners would have looked like approval of them. Fasting was a sign of mourning and of longing for God's deliverance, so Jesus' reply draws on wedding customs: nobody fasts at a wedding feast while the groom is present.

The woman with a flow of blood for twelve years was ritually unclean under Leviticus 15:25-27, and anything or anyone she touched became unclean. She touches the fringe of his cloak, the tassels that Numbers 15:37-41 commanded Israelites to wear as a reminder of God's commands. The mourners at the synagogue leader's house were part of normal funeral practice; a later rule in the Mishnah (the collection of rabbinic law compiled around AD 200) expects even a poor man to hire at least two flute players and a wailing woman for his wife's funeral. Cloth that had not been shrunk would tighten when washed and tear an old garment, and new wine still fermenting would stretch leather wineskins that had already been stretched and stiffened with use.
literary: The chapter carries on the pattern of chapter 8: the paralytic's healing closes the second group of three miracles, the call of Matthew and the questions about eating and fasting form a second interlude on discipleship, and a third group follows (the ruler's daughter together with the bleeding woman, the two blind men, and the mute man). Matthew tells the story of the girl and the woman as one scene with one nested inside the other, as Mark 5 and Luke 8 also do, but in far fewer words. Repeated phrases bind the chapter together: “Take courage” (verses 2 and 22), faith in verses 2, 22, and 29, and touching in verses 20, 25, and 29. The two reactions at the end, amazement from the crowds and accusation from the Pharisees, set out the choice that the rest of the Gospel presses on every reader.

outline.t: Matthew called; Jesus eats with sinners
The question about fasting; new wine, new wineskins
A ruler's daughter raised and a bleeding woman healed
A mute man freed; two responses
Compassion for the crowds and prayer for workers

doctrines.note: Jesus' first word to the paralytic is forgiveness, not healing, which shows what he takes to be the deepest human need. His call of Matthew and his meal with sinners show that God's mercy comes to those who know they need it: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

The Son of Man claims authority on earth to forgive sins, a prerogative Israel's teachers reserved for God, and backs the claim with a visible healing. Blind men call him Son of David, the royal title of the promised Messiah.

The chapter ends with the harvest: crowds harassed and helpless, and too few workers. Jesus tells his disciples to pray to the Lord of the harvest, and in the next chapter they become part of the answer.

words.note: Aphiemi, to release, let go, or forgive. The same verb can mean leaving a place or cancelling a debt. In verses 2, 5, and 6 it is the release of sins, the lifting of a weight God alone can lift, which is why the scribes hear blasphemy.

Eleos, mercy, the word the Greek Old Testament used for God's covenant love and kindness. Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”) against critics who kept the rules of the table but missed its purpose. Matthew is the only Gospel to include the quotation, and he uses it again in 12:7.

Splagchnizomai, to be moved with compassion. The word comes from the noun for the inner organs, which ancient people took as the seat of feeling, so it describes a gut-level response. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus or of figures in his parables who stand for God.

Kraspedon, the edge or fringe of a garment. Here it most likely means the tassels a faithful Jewish man wore at the corners of his cloak in obedience to Numbers 15. The woman reaches for the part of Jesus' clothing that marked him as a keeper of the law, and her touch, which should have spread uncleanness, is met with healing.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the one who brings God's forgiveness and God's future into the present. He speaks forgiveness in his own name, eats with sinners as a physician sits with the sick, and calls himself the bridegroom, an image the Old Testament uses for God in his love for Israel (as in Isaiah 62:5 and Hosea 2). His reference to the day when the bridegroom will be taken away is the first hint in Matthew of his death. The raising of the girl and the healing of the blind anticipate the resurrection life and the healed creation the prophets promised, and the new wine points to something that cannot simply be poured into the old forms. When he looks at crowds like sheep without a shepherd, he takes up Ezekiel 34, where God promises to shepherd his scattered flock himself and to set his servant David over them.

hard.q: Why does Jesus keep telling people not to spread the news of his miracles?
hard.a: In 8:4 and again in 9:30 Jesus orders silence, and in 9:31 the healed men ignore him. This pattern is even stronger in Mark, and nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholars debated it at length under the name of the messianic secret. Several explanations have been given. The most common is practical and political: popular hopes for the Messiah often centered on a warrior king who would drive out Rome, and a reputation as a wonder-worker could draw crowds with the wrong expectations, provoke the authorities, or make his work in the towns impossible, as Mark 1:45 says happened. A second explanation is theological: Jesus' identity could not be rightly understood until the cross and resurrection, so he held back open proclamation until then (compare Matthew 17:9). A third notes that Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a healer, since his mission centered on the kingdom and the forgiveness of sins. These reasons are not mutually exclusive, and many readers hold more than one.

questions: Jesus addressed the paralyzed man's sins before his body. What do you think people most need from God, and has that changed for you over time?
The Pharisees objected to the company Jesus kept. Whose company would a respectable religious person today avoid, and what would Jesus' meal with them look like?
Jesus saw the crowds as harassed and helpless. When you look at people in large numbers, what do you feel, and what would it take to see them as he did?
